'''''Cyperus eragrostis''''' is a species of [[Cyperaceae|sedge]] known by several common names, including '''tall flatsedge''', '''nutgrass''', '''tall nutgrass''', '''umbrella sedge''', '''chufa''', '''Earth almond''', '''zula nuts''', '''edible galingale''' and '''pale galingale'''.<ref name=":2">''Stevens, M., USDA, NRCS, & National Plant Data Cetnre. (n.d.).  Golden Nutsedge Cyperus eragrostis Lam. Retrieved from'' https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/pg_cyer.pdf</ref> In [[New Zealand]], it is also known by the [[Māori people|Māori]] name '''Puketangata.'''<ref name=":3">Flora of New Zealand | Taxon Profile | ''Cyperus eragrostis''. (2025). Retrieved March 25, 2025, from Nzflora.info website https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Cyperus-eragrostis.html</ref><ref name=":02">Cyperus eragrostis Lam. - Biota of NZ. (2024). Retrieved March 28, 2025, from Landcareresearch.co.nz website: https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/e8e994f0-60e0-4bba-b5ef-6455c6cd20be</ref> This species is associated with disturbed wet environments.<ref name=":12">NZOR Name Details - ''Cyperus eragrostis'' Lam. (2025). Retrieved March 26, 2025, from Nzor.org.nz website: https://www.nzor.org.nz/names/b6ded9c0-ccc6-4d3d-b0a0-fd984cb79555</ref>

==Description==
''Cyperus eragrostis'' is a tufted [[herbaceous plant]] in the sedge family that is commonly mistaken for a type of grass.<ref name=":02" /> However, it can be differentiated from grasses by many features. Firstly, the plant has a short, thick, woody [[rhizome]].<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":4">''Cyperus eragrostis''. (2024). Retrieved March 25, 2025, from New Zealand Plant Conservation Network website: https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/cyperus-eragrostis/</ref>  These stems are crucial for helping ''Cyperus eragrostis'' survive changes in seasons.<ref name=":5">Bouldjedri, M., Belair, G. D., Boualem Mayache, & Sebti, M. (2022). A new species for the vascular flora of Algeria: ''Cyperus eragrostis'' (Cyperaceae). ''Hacquetia'', ''21''(1), 187–195. https://sciendo.com/pl/article/10.2478/hacq-2021-0018</ref> These stems are [[trigonous]], solid, leafy, and a bit thicker at the base, growing 25-90 cm tall.<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":4" />

The [[leaves]] of the plant grow from the base and are slender, flat and linear with finely serrated margins.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6">I. Dakskobler, & B. Vreš. (2009). ''Cyperus eragrostis'' Lam. - A New Adventitious Species in the Flora of Slovenia. ''Hacquetia'', ''8''(1), 79–90. https://sciendo.com/pl/article/10.2478/v10028-009-0006-y</ref> They are usually flat but can also be slightly folded, forming a slight V-shape, often making them blend in with different species of grass.<ref name=":6" /> The leaf size ranges from a width of 4-8 mm and is typically bright green, while the protective sheaths of the plant are a dark purple-brown colour.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

The [[inflorescence]] of ''Cyperus eragrostis'' is another one of its most defining features and is the reason for one of its common names of “[[umbrella sedge]]”.<ref name=":3" /> At the top of the stem, a compound [[umbel]] can be found.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6" /><ref>Verloove, F., & El Mokni, R. (2021). First appointment of the invasive ''Cyperus eragrostis'' (Cyperaceae) as an established species in Tunisia. ''Flora Mediterranea'', ''31''. Page 83-88.

https://www.herbmedit.org/flora/FL31_083-088.pdf</ref> This compound umbel consists of up to twelve 3-10 cm rays which all have [[globose]] heads at the end of them.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> These globose heads (the rounded head at the end of a ray) have a diameter of 10-20 mm and are not a single flower. They are a cluster of small [[Spikelet|spikelets]] which 20-40 smaller flowers grow out of.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> These globose heads are surrounded by 5-8 much longer leaves for protection.<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />

The spikelets on the globose head are narrow, yellow, green or brown in colour, and range from 10 to 15 mm long.<ref name=":6" /> They can produce up to 40 bisexual [[florets]] per spikelet which are enfolded by a [[glume]].<ref name=":02" /> Each flower contains a single [[stamen]] and three stigma styles which are 1-1.2 mm long.<ref name=":5" /> Finally, after the process of [[Fertilisation|fertilization]], ''Cyperus eragrostis'' produces a fruit called an [[achene]]. This fruit is a trigonous, dry, hard-shelled fruit of a dark brown to black color ranging from 1.2 to 1.3 mm long.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

With all these features combined, ''Cyperus eragrostis'' is quite a simple and easy plant to spot, especially in the flowering seasons because it stands out from grasses for which it is often mistaken.
== Range ==
=== Natural global range ===
''Cyperus eragrostis'' is native to [[Subtropics|subtropical]] and [[Tropics|tropical]] regions of [[South America]], including [[Argentina]], [[Bolivia]], [[Brazil]], [[Chile]], and [[Peru]].<ref name=":7">Petřík, P. (2003). ''Cyperus eragrostis'' – A new alien species for the Czech flora and the history of its invasion of Euro. ''Preslia'' (75), Page 17-28. https://www.preslia.cz/P031CPet.pdf</ref> It has also been introduced to parts of [[Canada]], [[Mexico]], and parts of the [[United States]] including [[California]], [[Mississippi]], [[Louisiana]], [[New Jersey]], [[South Carolina]], [[Texas]], [[Oregon]], [[Pennsylvania]], and [[Washington, D.C.|Washington.]]<ref name=":5" />

Other than its native range, ''Cyperus eragrostis'' has spread to many different places around the world by being naturalized or introduced.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" /> It has been recorded as an invasive species in many European countries such as [[France]], [[Switzerland]], [[Germany]], [[Spain]], [[Hungary]], [[Netherlands]], [[Portugal]], [[England]], [[Italy]], [[Montenegro]], [[Czech Republic]], [[Slovenia]], [[Bulgaria]], and [[Turkey]].<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" /> This species is found scattered throughout the [[North Island|North]] and [[South Island|South Islands]] of [[New Zealand]]<ref name=":02" /> where it is also considered an invasive pest on the New Zealand weed list.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":8">Mcalpine, K., & Howell, C. (2024). ''List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024''. Retrieved from https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf</ref>

==Habitat==
''Cyperus eragrostis'' occupies various habitats around the world. It thrives in wet, open, disturbed environments made up of [[Hydric soil|hydric soils]] (saturated soils) such as wetlands, ditches, roadside ditches, riverbanks, ponds, swamps, floodplains, mud flats, shallow vegetated channels in pastures and fields, sandflats, and muddy lake edges.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":5" /> This species is a heliophilous plant, which means it thrives in areas of high sunlight and minimal shade.<ref name=":5" /> It is also sensitive to salinity (dissolved salts in water) and prefers moderate to high nutrient-rich soils with a neutral pH.<ref name=":5" /> ''Cyperus eragrostis'' is also able to establish itself in clay-loam and sandy-loam soils, making it easy for it to spread and reproduce.<ref name=":5" /> ''Cyperus eragrostis'' gets its nutrients through its roots so therefore the species prefers mesotrophic soil (soil with balanced nutrients) with a high richness of organic matter.<ref name=":5" /> With all these reasons combined, ''Cyperus eragrostis'' has been able to establish itself easily all around the world in both natural and modified environments.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" />

==Ecology==
===Life cycle and phenology===
''Cyperus eragrostis'' is great at establishing itself quickly because it has two main ways of reproduction; one through the sexual reproduction of seeds and one from spreading vegetatively through its rhizomes.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" /> The vegetative growth stage starts in spring from either seed germination or resprouting from a rhizome.<ref name=":2" /> Given the right conditions, during the end of spring and throughout summer, flowers and a small hard achene fruit will start to be produced on the compound umbels of spikelets.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" /> In late summer, the fruiting process will begin to end, with seeds waiting to be dispersed.<ref name=":5" /> These fruits/seeds have a high germination rate<ref name=":7" /> so when it was introduced to many countries for decorative and recreational uses<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":7" /> it spread quickly. The species has also managed to reproduce in large numbers through their rhizomes, therefore aiding its numbers in moist disturbed environments.<ref name=":5" />
===Predators, parasites and diseases===
There is very little information about the predators, parasites, and diseases of ''Cyperus eragrostis''. However, the seeds of the plant are important because they provide feed for many animals such as ducks, sandhill cranes, crows, and [[waterfowl]].<ref name=":2" /> In some countries, even mammals such as kangaroos and rats eat the seeds.<ref name=":2" /> Animals and birds also disperse its seeds quickly.<ref name=":2" /> The plant's tubers are also eaten by ducks and geese during the winter.<ref name=":2" />

==Cultural uses==
In some regions, the small nut-like tubers of ''Cyperus eragrostis'' are eaten by people either raw or cooked.<ref name=":2" /> This is not a common practice because it is considered an invasive weed in most countries where it is found but, when cooked, it tastes like coconuts and raisins.<ref name=":2" /> The base of the stem (rhizomes) are also edible.<ref name=":2" />

The leaf of ''Cyperus eragrostis'' was used by Native Americans to weave baskets and other objects.<ref name=":2" />

One possible reason for introducing this species is that it is good at controlling erosion. The rhizome of the plant enables it to form dense clumps in soil that helps to stabilize and restore degraded areas. However, once ''Cyperus eragrostis'' is introduced, it has a habit of overtaking and out-competing other species.<ref name=":2" />
